This was a long chapter, but it introduced a lot of important concepts that I hope
will help you with your own game projects in the future. Over the years, I have made

refined motion in my games and other projects. Just a simple easing function can make
the movement of an object look graceful, excited, or lethargic, which is powerful when
you're trying to tune the feel of a game.

As you have learned in both paper and digital games, the tuning of numbers is critically
important and has a significant effect on experience. The following is a list of variables

■ _Hero: Change how movement feels.
■ Adjust the speed.

■ Weapons: Differentiate the weapons more.
■ Spread: The spread gun could shoot five projectiles instead of just three but
have a much longer delayBetZeenShots.

■ Weapons: Add additional weapons.

■ Laser: Instead of doing all of its damage at once, the laser does continuous

■ Missiles: Missiles could have a lock-on mechanic and have a very slow fire-rate
but would track enemies and always hit. Perhaps missiles could be a different
kind of weapon with limited ammunition that were fired using a different button
(i.e., not the space bar). (If you want something to definitely move from one
place to another in a specific amount of time while curving along the way, a
Bézier curve is a great way to do it!)
■ Swivel Gun: Like the blaster but actually shoots at the nearest enemy. However,
the damage would be very low.
■ Enemies: Add additional enemies. You could create countless kinds of enemies for
this game.

■ Allow some enemies to shoot.

In this chapter, you make the skeleton of your
first card game, a digital version of the popular
Tri-Peaks solitaire game. By the end of the
chapter, you'll have not only a basic version of a
working card game but also a great framework
for future card games you want to create. The
next chapter will make this game look much
prettier.

including using JSON configuration files,
making a WebGL build, and your first look at
Unity's 2D sprite tools.

What You Will Learn
This chapter covers several new concepts and reviews many others. These include:
■ Using JsonUtility to parse data from text files in the JSON (JavaScript Object Notation)
format
■ Working with pixel-based 2D graphics assets—known as Sprites—and managing
sprite layers and sortingOrders
■ Using Unity's ScriptableObjects for project configuration
■ Setting up for a WebGL build (though you actually do the build in the next chapter)
■ Creating a full deck of cards from just a few sprites
■ Developing a reusable card deck for use in any card game
■ Working with one of Unity's built-in C# Interfaces

the PROSPECTOR Game 899
The Prospector Game
This chapter introduces you to a generic playing card system that you can use to make
any game featuring a standard 52-card deck (without Jokers). The specific card game
you're going to make is a solitaire game called Prospector (see Figure 33.1) that my
company, Digital Mercenaries, initially designed in the early 2000s. Prospector is based
on the classic solitaire card game Tri-Peaks, and as such, the rules of both are the same,
except for two things:
1. The narrative premise of Prospector is that the player is digging down for gold,
whereas the premise of Tri-Peaks is that the player is trying to climb three mountains.
2. The objective of Tri-Peaks is just to clear all the cards. The objective of Prospector is
to earn points by having long chains of cards, and in the full game, gold and silver
cards can increase the value of the chain (more details on this later).
Prospector Initial Layout
To get a feel for Prospector, I encourage you to play a paper prototype of the game. So,
please grab a normal deck of playing cards (like a physical, real deck), and follow these
directions:
1. Remove the Jokers and shuffle the remaining 52 cards.
2. Lay out 28 of the cards as shown in Figure 33.2 (with randomized cards; please don't
choose the exact cards shown in the figure). All cards should be face-down except
for the top row. The card edges don't need to be touching, but the lower cards do

" mine " that our prospector will be excavating.
3. The rest of the deck forms a draw pile. Place it above the top row of cards face-down.
4. Draw the top card from the draw deck and place it face-up centered above the top
row of cards. This is the target card.
When you've done all this, your layout should look similar to Figure 33.2.

Prospector Rules
The rules of Prospector are pretty straightforward, but I still find it to be a really fun
game.
1. Any card in the mine that is either exactly one rank above or one rank below the
target card may be moved from the mine onto the target card, making it the new tar-
get. Aces and Kings wrap around, so an Ace can be played on a King and vice versa.
2. If a face-down card is no longer covered by any card from a higher row, turn it face-up.
3. If none of the face-up cards can be played on the target card, draw a card from the
draw pile and place it on the target card, making it the new target card.
4. If you can clear the mine, you win. If the draw pile is empty, and you can't clear the
mine, you lose.
We won't worry about scoring and silver or gold cards for this paper prototype, but they
are part of the digital version of the game.
Example of Play
The image in Figure 33.2 shows an example initial layout for Prospector. In the situation
shown, the player can initially play either the 9C (9 of Clubs) or the 7S (7 of Spades)
onto the 8H.
The amber and green numbers show two possible sequences of play. In the amber
sequence, the 9C is played, becoming the new target card. This allows the play of 8S,
8D, or 8C. The player chooses 8S because it will then reveal the card that was hidden

by 9C and 8S. Then the amber sequence continues with 7S and finally 8C. Then the run
would end because no additional cards could be played to the target card. The amber
or green run would both result in the new layout shown in Figure 33.3.
Figure 33.3 The Prospector example game after the first run
Now, because there are no more valid face-up cards to play from the tableau, the player
must draw a card from the draw pile to become the next target card.
Try grabbing a real deck of cards and playing the game a few times to get a feel for it.
After you've done so, we can get started with the chapter.
You can also play the Prospector game on this book's website or download it from the
Apple App store for iOS or Google Play store for Android.

Constructing Cards from Sprites
One of the most important aspects of this project is that we're going to procedurally
construct an entire deck of 52 cards from the sprite images that were imported. This will
make the final build size smaller and will give you a chance to see how JSON works.
The image in Figure 33.9 shows an example of how this will be done, using pip, decora-

the sprites that make up each card:
■ Decorators: The elements that appear in the corner of all cards (the suit and rank in
opposite corners of the card).
■ Pips: The larger suit icons that appear in the main area of the card (the three large
hearts in the middle of the three of hearts).
■ Ranks: The number or letter part of the decorators in the two corners of the card
(e.g., A, 2, 3, …, Q, K).

As you saw in Figure 33.9, we're going to be building these cards out of several sprites,

you to ScriptableObjects. A ScriptableObject is an object in the Project pane that can be
configured in the Inspector to hold data that is stored as a file in the Project pane. It dif-

the future, swapping out different instances of that ScriptableObject could allow us to
very easily swap out different deck art. Using a ScriptableObject is not strictly necessary
for this prototype, but it's another good example of separating various elements of your
game into small, specific chunks.
